The village sat at the bottom of a wide valley, where the river slowed and spread into a chain of shallow ponds. In summer the water warmed enough for children to wade across, and in winter it froze hard enough to walk on, though nobody trusted it until the old man from the mill had tested it with his cane. He had done this every year for as long as anyone could remember, and the day he declared the ice safe was treated as an unofficial holiday. Shops closed early. Someone always brought a kettle down to the bank and lit a fire in the same blackened ring of stones. It was the kind of tradition that nobody had started on purpose and nobody could imagine stopping.

That year the ice came late. The first snow melted within a day, and the second never settled at all. By the middle of January the ponds were still open water, grey and restless under a low sky, and the mill was quiet because the wheel had not stopped turning. People said the weather was strange, which was what people always said, but this time they said it with a slight edge, as if they suspected the weather of doing it on purpose.
